title: The Afterlife of Atlantis
description:
Explore how later writers and amateur scholars transformed an ancient philosophical story into the enduring search for a lost continent. Modern research continues to examine the text as an allegory.

Join us as we explore the history and legacy of this famous tale.

voice.narration: What if an ancient tale told by a philosopher was meant to be remembered rather than forgotten? Every trail of inquiry leads back to a specific written source. Plato composed the dialogues Timaeus and Critias around three hundred and sixty BC, which contain the earliest mentions of Atlantis. In Plato's account, Solon visited Egypt and spoke with priests at Sais between five hundred and ninety and five hundred and eighty BC. King Amasis came from the great city of Sais, located in the Egyptian Delta. The foundress of Sais is called Neith in the Egyptian tongue. An old Egyptian priest told Solon that the Hellenes had no old opinion handed down by ancient tradition. As the priest tells Solon, "you Hellenes are never anything but children, and there is not an old man among you." The ancient Egyptian constitution is recorded in sacred registers to be eight thousand years old. This transmission of memory points toward an island waiting to be explored. What geographical wonders wait inside this lost domain? In Plato's account, a primeval man named Evenor lived in a mountain in the centre of the land with his wife Leucippe and their daughter Cleito. The narrative describes how the god Poseidon reshaped this home by breaking the ground to enclose the hill. He created alternate zones of sea and land that encircled one another. According to the story, these formations included two rings of land and three of water shaped as if turned on a lathe. Beneath the earth, Poseidon brought up two springs of water, with one running warm and the other cold. The soil produced an abundance of every variety of food. The account further notes a fertile plain located in the middle of the island. The region also supported numerous animals, including many elephants alongside creatures living in rivers, lakes, marshes, and mountains. The god eventually divided the land among his sons, making Atlas the first king over the ocean and the territory. Let us look closer at the heart of this ancient capital. In the story, the capital of the realm featured concentric rings of water and land. These alternating zones were connected by bridges and tunnels. Workers bored a canal from the sea straight through to the outermost zone. Plato explains that the canal measured three hundred feet in width and one hundred feet in depth, with a length of fifty stadia. The city walls were coated in brass, tin, and orichalcum. Miners dug orichalcum out of the earth in many parts of the island. Builders quarried stone for their buildings that was white, black, and red. While quarrying, workers hollowed out double docks featuring roofs formed directly out of the native rock. Inside the temple, a golden statue showed the god standing in a chariot as the charioteer of six winged horses. The statue reached such a size that the head touched the roof of the building. A race-course of a stadium in width extended all round the island in length for horses to race in. Then the story turns to the kingdom's fall. What happens next brings an abrupt end to the island kingdom. In Plato's account, a conflict takes place nine thousand years before his time between prehistoric Athens and the empire of Atlantis. The story relates that prehistoric Athens repels the invasion. According to the narrative, earthquakes and floods strike during a single day and night. Both the Athenian warriors and Atlantis sink into the earth and sea. The dialogue explains that Greece experienced recurring destructions by fire and water. The text notes that the greatest destructions of mankind are brought about by the agencies of fire and water. The account teaches that repeated destructions leave only illiterate mountain herdsmen to restart civilization in Greece. Such stories raise the lingering question of where these traces might still hide today. What real world occurrences might have left an imprint on the legend? On the Aegean island of Thera, a volcanic eruption occurred circa 1600 BC. Centuries later, an earthquake triggered a tsunami that submerged the Greek city-state of Helike in the winter of 373 BC. Researchers propose that Plato may have drawn loose inspiration from occurrences such as the destruction of Helike. Scholars also suggest potential roots in Egyptian records concerning the Thera eruption, or perhaps the Sea Peoples invasion. Another suggestion points to the failed Athenian invasion of Sicily. There is no evidence confirming any direct connection. These proposed parallels remain speculative. The narrative about the island did not end with ancient philosophy. Later writers began to view the account through a different lens. Ignatius Donnelly published a book titled Atlantis: The Antediluvian World in eighteen eighty-two. This author popularized the belief in the island as a historical lost continent. Amateur scholars from the nineteenth century misinterpreted the allegorical narrative as historical tradition. Modern scholars interpret the text as a fictional island. Researchers also view the work as an allegory on the hubris of nations. The boundary between ancient philosophy and modern belief continues to blur in our imagination. Subscribe to our channel for more historical mysteries.
